subject: SpaceX took in $14.6B, will spend up to $40B
bodyMarkdown:
Tesla reports its third quarter after the close today, and the call worth reading first already happened on Tuesday night. SpaceX posted its first profitable quarter as a public company, then guided to spending more on data centres next quarter than it booked in total revenue this one, which tells you more about where the economy's money is going than anything Tesla says tonight.

## SpaceX is an AI company that also launches rockets

The numbers landed Tuesday after the close. Revenue was $14.58 billion, up 161% from a year earlier, which Investing.com attributed to Starlink and AI compute. Net income came in at $4.4 billion against a roughly $1 billion loss in the same quarter last year. Here is the line I did not expect: Fortune reported that AI revenue nearly tripled to $7.56 billion and passed Starlink for the first time since the company went public. Connectivity, which is mostly Starlink, brought in $5.25 billion. The rocket business, the part the company is named after, did $1.77 billion. Keep your head about that profit, though. Fortune also noted SpaceX is still down $413 million across the first nine months of the year, so one strong quarter has not made this a profitable company.

## The capital spending line is what I read twice

Capital spending hit $19.59 billion in the quarter, up from $6.88 billion a year earlier, and about $16.4 billion of it went into the compute segment the company calls SI. Then came the guidance. SpaceX told investors to expect $35 billion to $40 billion of capital spending in the fourth quarter, tied to faster construction at its Memphis and Southaven sites. Set that against $14.58 billion of quarterly revenue and you can see how large the bet is. SpaceX finished September with 1.7 gigawatts of **nameplate capacity**, the power its sites are wired to draw rather than what they actually pull, and Musk said he would be surprised to bring on less than 13 gigawatts by the end of 2027. I wrote on Monday about CoreWeave's bonds trading at distressed prices. SpaceX is buying the same chips with satellite subscription cash, and lenders are not treating those two borrowers anything alike.

## The merger is a governance question

On the call Musk confirmed both boards have formed a **special committee**, a group of independent directors who negotiate when the person sitting on both sides of a deal cannot, to examine merging SpaceX and Tesla. He said shareholders asked for them and that he is recused as a conflicted party, describing the arrangement as "an odd kabuki dance where two groups of people are talking." He also cooled it down, saying that to assume a merger is certain "would be overstating it." Fortune valued the combination at roughly $3.5 trillion. The detail I would hold onto is the voting math. Musk said a Tesla deal needs approval from half of all outstanding shares rather than half of the shares actually voted, and he called that "quite a high hurdle." In a retail-heavy stock, plenty of shares never get voted at all.

## The takeaway

Tesla reports after the close today, and Bloomberg's consensus looks for $28.13 billion of revenue, roughly flat on the year, with adjusted earnings of 44 cents a share. Listen for two things: whether Tesla names a compute spending figure of its own, and whether anyone touching the special committee says a word about terms. If you hold Tesla, the vote threshold Musk described is your real leverage, so read the proxy when it arrives instead of the headlines. My guess is that the merger stays talk for months, while that capital spending guide is the part still shaping things in January.
